stories.title: Iran attacks US bases in Jordan after US strikes Larak Island
stories.summary: IRGC says attack in southern Iran killed and injured several soldiers. Iran says it launched missiles at two US bases in Jordan following a US attack on Larak Island in southern Iran earlier on Sunday. In a statement reported by Iranian news agencies on Sunday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said the combined missile and drone operation, which it called “Punishment of the Aggressor”, hit the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan. The exchange of attacks is the first flare-up in violence between the two sides since late July. The IRGC said the strikes “destroyed the technical and repair infrastructure, as well as the enemy fighter deployment sites”, inflicting significant damage. No injuries at either of the bases have been reported. “Aggression and crimes will not solve the enemy’s desperation in attempting to weaken the Islamic Republic’s control over the Strait of Hormuz, and every attack will be met with even more devastating responses,” the statement said. Tehran had earlier promised to retaliate for Sunday’s attack on Larak Island. The strikes risk renewing the military confrontation as Washington shifts from its bombing campaign to a financial pressure strategy on Tehran, as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its seventh month. A US official told Al Jazeera that the US strikes had targeted launchers on Larak that were set to fire rockets carrying mines towards the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s Fars news agency said that the attack by the “American-Zionist enemy” killed and injured soldiers, without providing a figure. In recent weeks, Washington has been claiming control over the Strait of Hormuz, saying that millions of barrels of oil have passed through the waterway under US military protection despite Tehran’s blockade.

stories.title: Hormuz Strait traffic drops to five vessels crossing per day over weekend
stories.summary: The number of commodity vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz dropped to five per day over the weekend, shipping data showed. The real figures remain unclear as some vessels switch off their automatic identification system in order to evade attacks.

stories.title: KBO's Seoul rivals set for final 3-game series at historic stadium
stories.summary: The two Seoul-based rivals in South Korean baseball are set for their final regular-season series this week in the historic stadium that they share, while the battle for the top spot in the standings will continue into the final full month of the campaign. The LG Twins and the Doosan Bears will meet for a three-game set at Jamsil Baseball Stadium from Tuesday to Thursday. They are the co-tenants of the stadium that will be torn down after this year, with the Bears serving as the home team this week. This will be the final week in which the Korea Baseball Organization (KBO) teams will play a pair of regularly scheduled three-game sets. Starting Sept. 8, teams will play makeup games -- those that were rained out or canceled due to a record-breaking heat wave earlier this year -- against different opponents in different cities almost every day. The Twins-Bears series will be more than just about sentimentality, as both teams are jostling for postseason spots. The Twins are in fourth place at 64-51-1 (wins-losses-ties), trailing the Kia Tigers (63-50-2) by a fraction in winning percentage. The Bears (61-52-4) sit two games behind the Twins to hold down the fifth and final postseason spot and they can overtake their rival with a sweep this week. The Twins hold a 7-4-1 edge in their season series so far. The competition for first place is also heating up, reminiscent of 2021. Back then, the Samsung Lions and the KT Wiz finished the regular season with an identical record and needed a one-game tiebreaker to determine who would finish first and earn a bye to the Korean Series. The Wiz prevailed 1-0 then and went on to win the franchise's first championship as well.

stories.title: Seoul shares open sharply lower on Fed chief's hawkish comments
stories.summary: Seoul shares opened sharply lower Monday, tracking losses on Wall Street amid the possibility of an imminent rate hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve caused by hawkish comments from its chief last week. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 175.30 points, or 2.58 percent, to 6,618.58 at the opening bell. On Friday (U.S. time), the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.02 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 0.52 percent. In his first major speech as Fed chair, Kevin Warsh warned that inflation remains a concern, leaving the door open to further interest rate hikes at its annual Jackson Hole symposium in Wyoming on Friday.

stories.title: Court set to rule on Unification Church leader's bribery case involving ex-first lady
stories.summary: SEOUL, Aug. 31 (Yonhap) -- A Seoul district court was set to rule Monday on Unif...
article_sentences: A Seoul district court was set to rule Monday on Unification Church leader Han Hak-ja's bribery case that includes charges of giving luxury gifts to the wife of former President Yoon Suk Yeol.

The Seoul Central District Court was scheduled to hand down its verdict at 2:10 p.m. over allegations that Han gave a luxury necklace and a Chanel bag to then first lady Kim Keon Hee while requesting favors for the church via an intermediary in July 2022.

Special counsel Min Joong-ki's team has sought a 13-year prison term for the 83-year-old, arguing the case constituted a direct violation of the constitutional spirit of separation of religion and politics.
Han's other charges include colluding with former church officials to hand 100 million won (US$66,400) to then Rep.
Kweon Seong-dong of the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) in January 2022.
Min's team alleged Han sought Kweon's help in gaining favors for the church in the event of Yoon's election as president in March that year.
Yoon, then candidate of the PPP, went on to win the election.
The Supreme Court in July upheld a two-year prison term for Kweon after finding him guilty of accepting the illegal funds from the church, stripping him of his parliamentary seat.
Lawmakers lose their seats in the National Assembly if they are sentenced to a fine of 1 million won or heavier punishment for violating the Political Funds Act.

The special counsel team has also sought prison terms for others indicted in Han's case, including a 10-year sentence for a former aide to Han and a 3 1/2-year term for Yun Young-ho, a former head of the church's global headquarters.
Han has denied the allegations during her trial, accusing former church official Yun of acting on his own.
